bib.title: Large Dual Encoders Are Generalizable Retrievers

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Large Dual Encoders Are Generalizable Retrievers" (GTR). Jianmo Ni, Chen Qu, Jing Lu, Zhuyun Dai, Gustavo Hernández Ábrego, Vincent Y. Zhao, Yi Luan, Keith B. Hall, Ming-Wei Chang, Yinfei Yang (Google Research; Yang listed with Apple). EMNLP 2022, pages 9844–9855.

COVERAGE: I read all 45,235 of 45,235 chars. That covers every page: the body, Limitations (§10), Appendix A (Tables 7 and 8) and the references. I skimmed the references for origins. I also pulled the figure captions with figures.py.

CLAIMS
- claim: Scaling the T5 encoder from Base to XXL while keeping a fixed 768-d single-vector dot product raises out-of-domain BEIR NDCG@10 every step. Base sits below BM25 and XXL sits about 3.5 points above it.
  number: Avg w/o MS Marco NDCG@10: BM25 0.423; GTR-Base 0.416, Large 0.445, XL 0.453, XXL 0.458
  setup: BEIR, 18 datasets with MS Marco excluded from the average. Models were pre-trained on 2B community QA pairs, then fine-tuned on all of MS Marco with RocketQA hard negatives. All runs use a 768-d embedding, mean pooling and cosine similarity.
  quote: "Avg w/o MS Marco 0.423 0.434 0.237 0.389 0.415 0.410 0.431 0.416 0.445 0.453 0.458" (columns: BM25, docT5query, DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, GenQ, ColBERT, GTR-Base…XXL)
  where: Table 3, p.9848
- claim: The same pattern holds for Recall@100. Base is below BM25 and XXL is above it.
  number: BM25 0.598; GTR-Base 0.580; GTR-XXL 0.619
  setup: as above
  quote: "Avg w/o MS Marco 0.598 0.603 0.418 0.543 0.594 0.590 0.590 0.580 0.609 0.616 0.619"
  where: Table 8, p.9855
- claim: Fine-tuning on 10% of MS Marco matches or beats full-data out-of-domain performance for the pre-trained GTR models, even though in-domain scores drop.
  number: GTR-XXL zero-shot 0.465 (10%) vs 0.458 (100%); MS Marco in-domain 0.379 vs 0.442
  setup: Keeps 10% of the training queries along with their positive and hard-negative passages. Columns: GTR-FT Large, XL; GTR Large, XL, XXL.
  quote: "Zero-shot average NDCG@10 w/o MS Marco 10% 0.413 0.418 0.452 0.462 0.465 100% 0.412 0.433 0.445 0.453 0.458"; "it only needs 10% of MS Marco supervised data to match the out-of-domain performance of using all supervised data"
  where: Table 4, p.9848; Abstract
- claim: Pre-training on community QA pairs and fine-tuning on MS Marco are both needed. Pre-training alone is far behind, and fine-tuning alone is below the full model at every size.
  number: XXL zero-shot: GTR-FT 0.430, GTR-PT 0.332, GTR 0.458
  setup: The community QA set is 2B Reddit/StackOverflow-style pairs, trained for 800K steps. Fine-tuning runs 20K steps at batch 2048 with τ=0.01.
  quote: "Base 0.387 0.295 0.416 Large 0.412 0.315 0.445 XL 0.433 0.315 0.453 XXL 0.430 0.332 0.458"; "This results in 2 billion question-answer pairs that we use to pre-train the dual encoder."
  where: Table 5, p.9849; §4.1 p.9846
- claim: Even at XXL, BM25 still wins on several lexical or specialised BEIR tasks. The caption counts 5 such tasks.
  number: NDCG@10, BM25 vs GTR-XXL: Trec-Covid 0.656 vs 0.501; BioASQ 0.465 vs 0.324; Signal-1M 0.330 vs 0.273; Trec-News 0.398 vs 0.346; Touché-2020 0.367 vs 0.256
  setup: Table 3, zero-shot
  quote: "GTR-XXL catches-up/surpasses BM25 on another 5 tasks and only under-performs on the remaining 5." Rows: "Trec-Covid 0.656 … 0.501", "BioASQ 0.465 … 0.324", "Signal-1M 0.330 … 0.273", "Trec-News 0.398 … 0.346", "Touché-2020 0.367 … 0.256"
  where: Figure 4 caption p.9847; Table 3 p.9848
- claim: Scaling turns some datasets where BM25 used to beat dense models into dense wins. NFCorpus is the paper's example.
  number: XL 0.343 vs BM25 0.325 (+5.5% relative)
  setup: NDCG@10
  quote: "our Base model under-performs BM25 but the XL model outperforms BM25 by 5.5% (0.343 vs. 0.325)"
  where: §5.2 p.9848
- claim: Growing the model helps more than growing the embedding. Going from 768-d to 4096-d gives a minimal gain at any model size.
  number: dims tested 256, 768, 2048, 4096 (results shown only as a plot)
  setup: Fine-tuned on MS Marco with no pre-training. Scored on 6 OOD datasets: BioASQ, DBPedia, NQ, HotpotQA, Fever, SciFact.
  quote: "the performance gain is minimum from the di-mensionality of 768 to 4096"
  where: §6.5 p.9850–9851, Figure 7
- claim: GTR-Large already beats the earlier best dense model (TAS-B) and the best sparse model (docT5query) on average.
  number: Avg w/o MS Marco: TAS-B 0.415, docT5query 0.434, GTR-Large 0.445
  quote: "The GTR-Large model already outperforms the previous best dense retrieval model TAS-B, as well as the best sparse model DocT5Query."
  where: §5.2 p.9848; Table 3
- claim: Latency rises steeply with size. At XXL it is about the cost of a re-ranker.
  number: 17, 34, 96, 349 ms (Base to XXL)
  setup: batch size 1, input length 128
  quote: "We found the latency increases from 17 ms, 34 ms, 96 ms to 349 ms."
  where: §8 p.9851
- claim: The model sizes are encoder-only parameter counts.
  number: 110M / 335M / 1.24B / 4.8B
  quote: "#. of params 110M 335M 1.24B 4.8B"
  where: Table 1 p.9847
- claim: Fine-tuning on NQ instead of MS Marco generalises worse. The gap shrinks with scale, and GTR-Base fine-tuned on NQ beats DPR.
  number: DPR 0.237; GTR-Base-NQ 0.360; XL-NQ 0.407 vs XL-MS Marco 0.453
  quote: "DPR NQ 0.237 GTR-Base NQ 0.360 GTR-Large NQ 0.379 GTR-XL NQ 0.407 GTR-Large MS Marco 0.445 GTR-XL MS Marco 0.453"
  where: Table 6 p.9849
- claim: Larger models retrieve longer documents on several datasets. On Touché, XXL returns documents about twice as long as Base. Trec-Covid goes the other way, which may explain XXL's drop there.
  number: none
  where: §6.4 p.9850, Figure 6

LIMITS
- The authors' stated limitations: no distillation, English only. They quote: "we focus on standard dual encoder training and have not investigated other techniques such as distillation" and "we only focus on English-only corpus".
- The embedding-size ablation drops pre-training and uses only 6 datasets. The numbers exist only in a plot.
- The 10% data-efficiency result covers Large/XL/XXL only, has no variance or seeds, and uses only one subsample ratio.
- No significance tests appear anywhere.
- XXL is not monotone per dataset. Trec-Covid falls from 0.584 (XL) to 0.501 (XXL). Climate-Fever and SciFact also dip.
- Cost claims rest on a single latency measurement. Index size and throughput are not reported.
- No hybrid BM25+dense combination is tested.
- The 2B community QA pre-training corpus is not described beyond its sources.
- Dated: the baselines are 2021-era. Contriever (Izacard 2021) is compared only through Figure 5, on 15 datasets.

BUILDS ON
- Sentence-T5 (Ni et al., 2021): mean pooling of the T5 encoder.
- T5 (Raffel et al., 2020).
- In-batch sampled softmax (Henderson et al., 2017), applied bi-directionally (Yang et al., 2019).
- Hard negatives: RocketQA (Qu et al., 2021) for MS Marco, and Lu et al. (2021) for NQ.
- Benchmark: BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021).
- Baselines: DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020), ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), ANCE (Xiong et al., 2020), TAS-B (Hofstätter et al., 2021).
- The embedding-dimension observation is compared with Neelakantan et al. (2022).

CODE: No snippets. The loss is Eq. 1–2 (in-batch softmax over cosine similarity divided by τ, plus extra hard negatives), §3.1 p.9846. Checkpoints are at https://github.com/google-research/t5x_retrieval.

FIGURES
- Fig. 4, p.4 (printed 9847): "Comparison with BM25 on NDCG@10 …" Per-dataset bars for Base to XXL against BM25. It shows at a glance where scaling overtakes BM25 and where it doesn't.
- Fig. 7, p.8: "Average NDCG@10 for selected OOD datasets with different bottleneck and model sizes." One plot carries the model-size-vs-embedding-dim argument.
- Fig. 1, p.1: average Recall@100 and NDCG@10 against model size, showing the headline scaling trend.
- Fig. 2, p.2: architecture showing shared towers and a fixed 768-d embedding.

PROBLEMS
- Figure 4 text came out as unlabeled numbers. I used Table 3 instead.
- The "5 tasks" count conflicts with Table 3. By the table, XXL is also slightly below BM25 on Fever (0.740 vs 0.753), SciFact (0.662 vs 0.665) and HotpotQA (0.599 vs 0.603), which the caption treats as "catches-up". That makes 8 strictly lower, not 5.
- Bold markers for best results did not survive extraction.
- §8 writes "microseconds (ms)", so the latency unit is ambiguous. The values read like milliseconds.
- The abstract and intro say "up to 5 billion parameters", while Table 1 lists 4.8B.
- No embedded instructions were found.
